meeting_tip: Open with the outcome: 'By the end of this call we'll have decided X.'
On video, look at the camera, not the screen, when you make your key point.
Use the 'rule of three': summarise any update in three bullet points.
Pause for two seconds after asking a question; silence invites better answers.
Name people when you hand over: 'Priya, could you take the next bit?'
Raise your laptop so the camera is at eye level; it reads as confident.
Light from the front (a window or lamp behind the screen), never from behind you.
When you disagree, start with 'Help me understand…' rather than 'No, but…'.
End every meeting with owners and dates: who does what by when.
Mute when not speaking, but unmute early so you don't miss your cue.
Use people's names twice in a conversation; it builds rapport.
If a meeting overruns, offer to take the rest offline with the two people who need it.
Paraphrase before you answer: 'So the question is whether…' It buys time and shows listening.
Smile in the first five seconds on camera; tone carries more than words.
Share a single slide or doc, not your whole screen, to avoid notification surprises.
Lead with numbers: '3 incidents, down from 7' beats 'fewer incidents'.
Keep status updates to 60 seconds: done, doing, blocked.
Credit others publicly and specifically: 'Ravi's fix cut alerts by half.'
Prepare one smart question for any meeting with senior leaders.
Write the decision in the chat before the call ends so everyone sees the same thing.
Speak 10% slower than feels natural on video; audio lag makes fast talk hard to follow.
Use a headset; good audio matters more than a good camera.
Turn 'I think' into 'The data shows' wherever you can.
When you get a question you can't answer, say 'Good question, I'll come back by 3 pm.'
Sit upright and lean slightly forward; it signals engagement on camera.
Avoid filler ('basically', 'actually', 'like'). A short pause sounds more confident.
Start on time even if people are missing; it trains everyone to be punctual.
If you chair, invite the quietest person to speak first on a topic.
Use 'we' for problems and 'they' when crediting others' wins.
Close with a one-line recap; people remember the last thing they hear.
